articles.content: Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Pauline Hanson has released a statement this morning welcoming South Australian senator Leah Blyth to her party . Blyth is the second high-profile federal defection from the Coalition to One Nation – after Barnaby Joyce . Senator Blyth will be One Nation’s first South Australian Senator and will build on One Nation’s expanding support within the state. My team and I are delighted to welcome Senator Blyth to sit in the Senate with One Nation. We are facing at the next election clearly a coalition of the Liberals, Nationals and One Nation, with all the baggage that each of these parties brings to the table. articles.content: Deagreez/Getty Images Most Australians are using – or at least have tried out – generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini, among many others. We can use them to search for information, answer questions, and generate text, images, sound and video. As generative AI becomes more sophisticated and ubiquitous, many people are no longer able to distinguish AI-generated content from authentic, human-made content. Our new representative survey of 2,000 Australian adults conducted in August and September 2026 found 76% of Australians had recently encountered content they initially believed was real, only to later discover it had been generated by AI. The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognise it at all. The synthetic trap People with high levels of education who are interested in the technology and have high AI literacy, are the most likely to report having mistaken AI content for real. However, this doesn’t mean these groups are more exposed or susceptible to AI-generated content. Instead, the data suggests these people are better at recognising when they’ve been misled. In fact, people with low education and lower AI literacy are the most likely to say they don’t know whether they have mistaken AI content for real. Therefore, many Australians may not recognise when they have encountered synthetic content. This presents a dilemma for users who are increasingly turning to AI tools to seek information. Trust in AI is low While AI use has grown rapidly, many are sceptical of the technology and concerned about how it might impact on society. About half (51%) of Australian respondents said they use AI chatbots or tools at least weekly, and more than one quarter (28%) use them daily. Almost everyone (96%) is aware of at least one generative AI platform. Despite widespread awareness and usage, trust in major AI tools remains very low. When asked “how much do you trust or distrust generative AI chatbots or tools?”, only a minority said they trust ChatGPT (34%), Microsoft Copilot (24%), Google Gemini (24%) and Claude (17%). Our survey also shows people are particularly distrusting of politicians and social media companies that use generative AI. More than half of Australians believe the use of AI by politicians and political parties will make society worse, with social media companies and news media viewed almost as negatively. In contrast, the report reveals that people view scientists and healthcare professionals as the most trustworthy and benevolent users of AI, with around half saying their use of the technology will improve society. How do people verify content? Despite this high level of exposure to AI-generated content and low levels of trust, people rarely use proactive measures to identify or verify if content was AI generated. When people suspect AI-generated content, the majority simply take a closer look and examine the content carefully, relying on their intuition. Some check comments made by other online users. But few people look for disclosure statements or labels to identify whether it was made with AI and even fewer turn to trusted sources of news. Rather than engaging in lateral reading – leaving the content and checking independent sources – most people engage in vertical reading, which involves only looking within the source. They scrutinise the content itself and rely on their own judgement. This approach becomes less effective as AI-generated content becomes increasingly convincing. Generally, younger people are more likely to check whether information is true, using a range of verification strategies. The exception is checking a trusted news source, which is more common among those aged 45 and over. Instead, young adults are far more likely to look at comments from other users than older age groups. Additionally, AI literacy plays an important role in people’s verification strategies. Those with high AI literacy are much more likely to closely examine content than those with low understanding of the technology, suggesting that education about how AI works supports more active and critical evaluation of online information. People want strong safeguards Because of the low levels of trust in the technology, Australians say they want strong safeguards around it. Most importantly, they want protections to ensure the accuracy and reliable responses when they are using an AI platform. They also want guardrails in place to prevent AI from generating illegal, dangerous or harmful content, and protections to reduce the presence of bias and ensure fairness and equity in the content it generates. This points to the need for a multi-pronged response from the tech platforms and government. First, digital platforms need clearer and more consistent labelling of AI-generated content. If people are expected to make informed decisions about what they’re seeing, they need transparent information about where that content comes from. Second, the findings show people with higher levels of AI literacy are better equipped to recognise synthetic content and engage in more critical evaluation practices. We need to educate all Australians with media and AI literacy. Education in schools is important, but adults need training too. We need a whole-of-society approach where adults can have access to education through local community or workplace initiatives. Australia already lags behind other countries when it comes to media literacy education and the rapid increase in AI only makes the need for a national approach more urgent. articles.author: Doosie Morris
articles.content: It started as a joke, but Tightarses of Melbourne has grown into a thriving community. Accompanied by its founder Lisa Lorenz, Guardian Australia tests how much bang you can get for $50 Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email In 2022 Lisa Lorenz was working in music promotion when the overpriced culinary options and long lines at Melbourne’s Moomba festival led her and her partner to Clocks, the much passed over pokies-cum-tavern at Flinders Street station. The cocktails were $10 and the vibe on the bustling terrace was surprisingly satisfying. “It’s the kind of place most people would never think to go, but we were having such a great afternoon, chatting to people and watching the world go by,” she tells me. As the drinks continued to flow the pair were compelled to spread the good word. They took a few “intentionally terrible photos”, created an Instagram page and Tightarses of Melbourne, a guide to the city’s scrimpiest food and drink specials, was born. Continue reading...

The cocktails were $10 and the vibe on the bustling terrace was surprisingly satisfying. “It’s the kind of place most people would never think to go, but we were having such a great afternoon, chatting to people and watching the world go by,” she tells me. As the drinks continued to flow the pair were compelled to spread the good word. They took a few “intentionally terrible photos”, created an Instagram page and Tightarses of Melbourne, a guide to the city’s scrimpiest food and drink specials, was born. Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Tightarses is for the people’: a happy hour crawl with Melbourne’s cheapest guide

articles.author: Rod Sims
articles.content: Fossil fuel companies are effectively not paying for the natural resource on which their businesses depend Raising more tax revenue from our gas industry is the closest thing you will find to a public policy no-brainer . There are numerous calls for the government to return the budget to surplus quickly, in contrast to the current forecasts of continuing budget deficits well into the future. Those calling for a return to surplus generally want large net expenditure cuts, which are difficult given the pressure to spend more on an ageing population and on defence, just to name two areas. I believe this will only succeed if, in addition to better control of expenditure, there is focus on the revenue side. In this context, by far the easiest step is to collect more tax from our gas industry . Continue reading...

articles.content: NASA/JPL/NGA , CC BY-SA The 600-kilometre Alpine Fault is one of New Zealand’s largest earthquake hazards. In our new study , we used fibre optic cables to map the fault in unprecedented detail to show how future earthquakes might unfold. The Alpine Fault runs the length of the Southern Alps and defines the boundary between the Australian and Pacific tectonic plates. It has been the focus of extensive geological , seismological and drilling investigations in recent years because it produces very large (magnitude 7-8) earthquakes about every 300 years. With the most recent earthquake in 1717, scientists estimate there’s a 75% chance of a large one in the next 50 years , with high odds it will be larger than magnitude 8. In anticipation of that event, several research groups are working hard to understand how the Alpine Fault is being loaded prior to its next rupture and how its geometry and physical characteristics may affect an earthquake’s propagation and the resulting ground shaking. Our focus is on determining the fault’s geometry and internal structure at scales much finer than can be studied using conventional seismometers, which are usually spaced tens of kilometres apart. Instead we used a standard telecommunications cable to reveal the fault’s internal detail. Our study shows the fault is not a single clean crack but rather a band of damaged rock about 200 metres wide. The Alpine Fault is a wide band of damaged rock, with narrower zones where it likely slipped. Author provided , CC BY-SA Within it, we found six much narrower zones of more intensely crushed and sheared rock. We call these “cores” and think the most prominent core is where the fault slipped during recent large earthquakes. This matters because an earthquake’s size depends mainly on how much of the fault breaks. Understanding the fault’s structure helps us work out how much could break at once, and how large the next big earthquake might be. Lighting up the Alpine Fault We send pulses of laser light down an optical fibre in a cable installed by telecommunications company Chorus near Haast. This turns the cable into a long line of sensitive earthquake sensors. We used a technique called distributed acoustic sensing ( DAS ). This records microscopic vibrations of the cable by measuring how each laser pulse is scattered by atomic-scale imperfections in the glass fibre. Our measurements show seismic waves produced by nearby small earthquakes travel along the fault as distinctive energy pulses known as fault zone guided waves. The propagation of these waves along a fault is similar to how light travels along an optical fibre. The fault zone guided waves we have recorded reveal the discrete cores, only about 10 metres wide, within the 200-metre zone of damaged rock. A fibre-optic cable near Haast recorded earthquake waves guided by the Alpine Fault, revealing several narrow fault cores within a wider zone of damaged rock. The circle size shows earthquake magnitude. Green circles mark earthquakes with clear guided waves, and orange circles mark those with less distinct guided waves. Voon Hui Lai , CC BY-SA Our observations suggest one of the cores extends continuously for about 180 kilometres along the Alpine Fault, from Martins Bay at least as far as Karangarua. While the fault bends and kinks at the surface, our new measurements imply that, deep underground, its main slip zone appears to be largely continuous. Whether slip occurs on a single smooth surface, as our observations suggest, or on separate, discontinuous fault structures likely influences the extent and direction of rupture, and hence the ground shaking it produces. Significantly, the most prominent core extends across a distinct change in the Alpine Fault’s geometry near Martyr River. There the dipping geometry characteristic of the fault along much of the West Coast alters to a steeper, almost vertical geometry extending towards Milford Sound. Earlier research suggests many past earthquakes have started or stopped near Martyr River. Determining which factors control the start and end of an earthquake along the Alpine Fault, including whether slip occurs on a single, continuous surface or jumps between separate faults, is crucial to understanding the likely extent of future ruptures. This in turn determines the earthquake’s overall magnitude and resulting ground shaking. Another recent study used grooves scratched onto a fault plane, known as “slickenlines”, to show the Alpine Fault ruptured from south to north in the last large earthquake in 1717. If a future Alpine Fault quake were to rupture in a south to north direction, it would cause higher-intensity shaking in the populated regions of Canterbury, Marlborough, Tasman and the northern West Coast. In contrast, a north to south rupture would propagate towards Fiordland, where fewer people live. The DAS measurements we made at Haast enable us to describe the fine-scale internal structure of the Alpine Fault at depths relevant to earthquake nucleation and propagation. Together with other studies, we are building a clearer picture of how different sections of the fault are connected in locations where large earthquakes appear to preferentially start or stop. Our observations will provide vital information for future models of rupture progression and the radiation of seismic energy that causes ground shaking. Understanding this will help New Zealand prepare for the hazard and the impacts of future Alpine Fault earthquakes. John Townend has received funding from the Catalyst and Marsden funds, both administered by the Royal Society Te Apārangi; the Natural Hazards Commission Toka Tū Ake; and the Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment. He serves as chair of the publications committee of the Seismological Society of America. Meghan S. Miller receives funding from the Australian Research Council and from National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) in her role as program director of AuScope Earth Imaging. Voon Hui Lai receives funding from Singapore Ministry of Education (MOE) AcRF Tier 3b project “Investigating Volcano and Earthquake Science and Technology (InVEST)”.

The circle size shows earthquake magnitude. Green circles mark earthquakes with clear guided waves, and orange circles mark those with less distinct guided waves. Voon Hui Lai , CC BY-SA Our observations suggest one of the cores extends continuously for about 180 kilometres along the Alpine Fault, from Martins Bay at least as far as Karangarua. While the fault bends and kinks at the surface, our new measurements imply that, deep underground, its main slip zone appears to be largely continuous. Whether slip occurs on a single smooth surface, as our observations suggest, or on separate, discontinuous fault structures likely influences the extent and direction of rupture, and hence the ground shaking it produces. Significantly, the most prominent core extends across a distinct change in the Alpine Fault’s geometry near Martyr River. There the dipping geometry characteristic of the fault along much of the West Coast alters to a steeper, almost vertical geometry extending towards Milford Sound. Earlier research suggests many past earthquakes have started or stopped near Martyr River. Determining which factors control the start and end of an earthquake along the Alpine Fault, including whether slip occurs on a single, continuous surface or jumps between separate faults, is crucial to understanding the likely extent of future ruptures. This in turn determines the earthquake’s overall magnitude and resulting ground shaking. Another recent study used grooves scratched onto a fault plane, known as “slickenlines”, to show the Alpine Fault ruptured from south to north in the last large earthquake in 1717. If a future Alpine Fault quake were to rupture in a south to north direction, it would cause higher-intensity shaking in the populated regions of Canterbury, Marlborough, Tasman and the northern West Coast. In contrast, a north to south rupture would propagate towards Fiordland, where fewer people live. The DAS measurements we made at Haast enable us to describe the fine-scale internal structure of the Alpine Fault at depths relevant to earthquake nucleation and propagation. Together with other studies, we are building a clearer picture of how different sections of the fault are connected in locations where large earthquakes appear to preferentially start or stop. Our observations will provide vital information for future models of rupture progression and the radiation of seismic energy that causes ground shaking. Understanding this will help New Zealand prepare for the hazard and the impacts of future Alpine Fault earthquakes. articles.content: New tariffs planned as Trump administration clamps down on ‘unfair trade practices’ Hannah Webster , senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation , also called for other measures. The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances. The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out. Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home. Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.content: Unai Emery wanted the winger but, like Harvey Elliott last season, he has been left out in the cold despite Villa’s attacking struggles It is three years this week since Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring for Manchester United in a 3-3 draw at Galatasaray in the Champions League, on a typically boisterous night in Istanbul when Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, now his teammates at Aston Villa, were also among the starters. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award. He went on to score twice at Old Trafford on Boxing Day, in a 3-2 victory against Villa, and a couple of months later his double at home to West Ham was the catalyst for that iconic celebration photo of Garnacho, Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund sitting on the advertising hoardings at the Stretford End, beaming smiles all round. All three were at the heart of United’s plans for a bright future, beacons of hope. At the end of that season, Garnacho signed off in style, he and Mainoo scoring against Manchester City at Wembley to win the FA Cup . Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Early in the second half of Tuesday night’s National League South match between Torquay United and Chesham, play was briefly suspended due to an ear-splitting din emitted over the Plainmoor public address system. “The game has stopped because the Torquay Tannoy system is making a loud noise that won’t stop,” posted Chesham on their Social Media Disgrace account. “I’m not kidding.” A sort of aural cross between an ocean liner’s foghorn and a party conference speech delivered by a senior member of the Reform party, it eventually stopped and play resumed with Torquay running out 2-1 winners. In this constantly changing world of global disruptions, uncertainties and risks, with social, political and economic disaffection seemingly on the rise everywhere, it’s genuinely heartening to know that some things never change . ‘Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose’, as the late, great French writer Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr famously said, something that I’m sure Big Dunc is well aware of” – Noble Francis. May I be the 1,092nd correspondent to demand a review of the Letter o’ the Day award for Monday – and it be awarded to Declan Hackett for his letter foretelling the rescinding of the red card given to Lenny Yoro on Sunday? Given the precedent of awarding/revoking/re-awarding of the Afcon 2025 edition this would be entirely justified” – Peter Martin. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.content: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. Continue reading...

I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. articles.content: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford. This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

articles.content: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. Continue reading...

Russo is perhaps best known for co-creating the spy comedy series Danger 5, which had an aesthetic inspired by 60s and 70s men’s magazines; The Fox has a similarly thick retro texture. I love how this film feels as though it was made in consultation with the animal world, taking place in a universe where animals can speak to humans – though that’s perhaps the least weird thing about it. articles.author: Martin Pegan
articles.content: One or perhaps more spots are up for grabs ahead of the summer series against New Zealand. We assess the leading batters’ chances of being picked in the XI Australia’s cricketers would be within their rights to be counting down the days until attention turns to the first Test of the home summer against New Zealand in Perth. As the sandpapergate scandal overshadows a pair of white-ball series against arch-rivals England, batters around the country have been pressing their claims for a place in Australia’s XI when the Chappell-Hadlee Trophy series begins on 9 December. A vacancy has already opened at the top of the order after selectors took the unusual step to confirm earlier this month that Marnus Labuschagne had been dropped from the squad for the four-Test series. The race to replace Australia’s No 3 – whether slotting straight into Labuschagne’s spot at first drop or as part of a batting order reshuffle – has become packed with Test discards and an emerging talent hoping to earn a debut. The door could open for more than one addition to the XI alongside presumed incumbents Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and wicketkeeper Alex Carey, with worrying signs Australia’s ageing squad is starting to creak after three defeats in their past five Tests. Continue reading...

articles.author: Osasu Obayiuwana in Lagos
articles.content: After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history. As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday , was a “big joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute. Continue reading...

articles.content: The job of Mauricio Pochettino’s successor is to fine-tune a team on the up. That requires a bureaucrat rather than a figurehead First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it. But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work . Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Downie
articles.content: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

articles.content: Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee By Wisden Cricket Monthly Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. articles.content: Vivienne Foroughirad/Texas A&M/Shark Bay Dolphin Research Project In the turquoise waters of Western Australia’s Shark Bay lives a large resident population of dolphins. Some of these marine mammals are 54 years old, others just infants. But no matter their age, they live highly social lives. Researchers have studied these dolphins for decades . Forty years on, our extensive dataset reveals crucial insights into how these animals socialise throughout their lives – and how their social choices affect their health and fitness. In our new study , published in PLOS Biology, we analysed nearly 40 years of data on over 450 wild Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins ( Tursiops aduncus ) from Shark Bay. We found that as dolphins navigate their social world, they develop unique personalities and social preferences, and individuals who are consistent about these preferences may live longer. Sociality is a spectrum Dolphins’ social lives mirror our own in remarkable ways. As they navigate their blue world, dolphins move in and out of social groups, constantly making decisions about who to spend time with and who to avoid, depending on the task at hand. Much like humans, dolphins vary markedly in how social they are. Research shows some are more cliquish, while others are true social butterflies, embedded in large and complex social networks These differences matter. Just as in humans and many other species, the way dolphins navigate their social lives can shape their survival, longevity and reproductive success. For example, strong social connections promote resilience, while social isolation can increase mortality risk . Such patterns are not set in stone either. In many species , including humans, social behaviour is shaped as we age. In humans, social networks often become smaller, with older adults becoming more selective, investing their time and energy in a smaller number of meaningful relationships. But what happens as dolphins age? Previous research on dolphins has shown us that extended maternal care in older dolphin mothers is evidence of reproductive senescence – similar to menopause in humans. This raises an intriguing question: do dolphins also show other patterns of ageing like our own? Drone footage of six individuals who reside in nearshore habitat off the coast of Monkey Mia, Shark Bay. In front from left to right are Risotto (24) and her calf, Linguini (2), who is in a nursing position; Whoops (27), and Wags (6). Behind them are two more individuals; Risotto’s previous calf Arancini (6), and Jungle (8). Diana Alvarado/Shark Bay Dolphin Research Project , CC BY Social ageing can be measured in multiple ways As we age, we develop personalities, build and lose relationships, and create our unique social environment which changes with each passing year. This process of social change as we grow is called social ageing . Most studies of social ageing have examined how individuals change over time by collecting many measurements, then finding their average. This can be useful for dolphins that have only a few close companions. But for those who frequently join groups large and small, an average tells us very little. We can instead turn to another measurement: predictability . This describes the spread of an individual’s data. Those dolphins who consistently spend time with the same number of other dolphins are very predictable. Those who flit between groups of many sizes are much less predictable. Predictability is difficult to measure because it requires a single individual be measured dozens, even hundreds, of times. Luckily, with 40 years of data on over 450 dolphins, research can go beneath the surface to study not only how individuals change in sociability with age on average, but how predictable they are, and if predictability can change, too. Being consistent is key For our new study, we examined the effects of sex, age, and individual personality on group size (a measure of sociability) throughout the population of dolphins at Shark Bay. We discovered several key points. First, dolphins follow a pattern very similar to humans and other long-lived species: they increase their average group size with age, to a point. After that point, which is unique to each individual, those average group sizes begin to decrease. Second, regardless of what their average group size is, individuals become more predictable with age. Third, males had a higher average group size and higher predictability than females. Finally, individuals who continued to increase their group size average and predictability most with age lived longer. Social stability can being a sustaining force Our research into dolphins’ social lives suggests that developing a strong and stable social environment can buffer many of the effects of ageing and enhance lifespan. Studying dolphins’ social traits reveals that it’s not only average behaviour which shapes fitness outcomes, but individual predictability. To truly understand how ageing shapes us, we must look beyond the average to see how the predictability of our social decisions can affect us as we navigate our world. This study reinforces the importance of maintaining consistent social relationships throughout the ageing process. In the case of the Shark Bay dolphins, it’s not only about how large one’s social circle is; rather, it’s about the social circle staying roughly the same size and type over size. And this holds an important lesson for us, because the trends we find in dolphins closely parallel the sort of patterns we see in human social behaviour as well. This project has received grant funding from the National Science Foundation and the US Office of Naval Research, as well as material support from the Royal Automobile Club Monkey Mia Resort. Celine Frere receives funding from the Australian Research Council and the US National Science Foundation. Janet Mann receives funding from The National Science Foundation for the long-term Shark Bay dolphin research.

articles.author: Anna Spargo-Ryan
articles.content: Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s tribute to Molly Meldrum contained heaps of the right words. But they were written by something that can’t feel I know how this will sound but when my nanna died the second thought I had, after utter devastation, was: “This is a writer’s dream.” She was 101. That is so many years old. I wrote the eulogy to end all eulogies, breaking my own heart with a bottomless well of memories, anecdotes and in-jokes. It was achingly personal and exquisitely her. The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team took a similar approach in this week’s tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum , by which I mean they generated it with AI. I imagine the conversation went something like: we are 25 years old, who even was she? And then one of them plugged Molly’s name into Claude while the others went downstairs for $11 coffees. Job done. Continue reading...

articles.content: Australia is currently in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) over potentially flying Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. If accepted, Bennell-Pegg – who is the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency and completed ESA training in 2024 – would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut. To “buy a seat” on a space mission, Australia has to make a financial contribution to the ESA. The precise sum is not public, but reports claim it could exceed the A$100 million mark . There has been interest in the press and excitement among space advocates. Many are pointing out that sending a home-grown astronaut to space would yield potential benefits to industry and the nation as a whole, inspiring younger generations. There would be a powerful symbolism in sending an Australian woman to space. However, while human spaceflight can deliver substantial benefits, it’s costly. As we’re in the midst of a substantial public campaign to #FlyKatherine , it’s crucial to properly analyse some of the claims being made about the potential benefits of such an expensive proposal. What counts as an Australian astronaut? The discussion raises an interesting point about what constitutes an Australian astronaut. To date, five Australian-born people have flown to space, two as NASA astronauts and three privately. The most recent was physicist Elaine Hyde, the first Australian woman in space . But her 2025 Blue Origin flight was privately funded, and she hasn’t been given the label of the first “female Australian astronaut”. The federal government hasn’t signalled a strong interest in flying an Australian astronaut. Science minister Tim Ayres unequivocally said state and territory governments and private industry would have to pitch in. However, only South Australia has agreed to contribute; industry has pledged up to $6 million. The Northern Territory called the proposal “ reckless ”. These debates are not new. In the 1980s, the Hawke government announced it would send an Australian astronaut on the space shuttle. However, then Minister for Science, Barry Jones, noted it wasn’t a high priority . Prestige and public relations were not considered reason enough when government spending was to be reined in. The cost would be substantial We don’t know if Australians would support spending $100m on a single space mission while facing a cost-of-living crisis. When surveyed in 2025, 51.5% of Australians supported government investment in an astronaut programme, but respondents were not given a cost. Generally speaking, once government programs reveal their costs , public support decreases. When asked in 2023 , more Australians supported the cancellation of a $1.2 billion Earth observation satellite than disagreed with it being canned. Would these funds be better deployed within the space sector? Currently the Australian Space Agency’s funding is $21.7m over two years. The cost of flying a single Australian astronaut would fund a decade for the agency. Put another way, $100m is half of the total government investment in space or space adjacent companies in the last 18 months. Space science and research occurs at universities, in government agencies, and in private industry; many organisations have sent experiments to space, often relatively cheaply. Advocates have argued there would be significant benefits to Australia. There’s no doubt space is of immense benefit to industry and the nation, from banking to navigation to farming . An astronaut can’t meet all these needs, and we don’t know how they fit into our long-term plans. Australia doesn’t have a whole of government space policy and an astronaut is not a space program. The suggestion that Australia’s growing space industry would stand to gain similarly deserves deeper analysis. How and where specifically will funds flow back to Australia? Does the public think supporting industry is a reason to send an astronaut to space? ESA has a geographic return policy which sees member states receive industrial contracts proportional to how much they pay ESA. But Australia is not a paying member state, and not looking to be. The $100 million includes training, equipment and launch; it’s difficult to see how the bulk of those funds will be spent in Australia rather than in Europe, where ESA is based. What about inspiration? Representation matters, particularly for encouraging girls and young women to pursue careers in space. Bennell-Pegg’s selection and training have already inspired Australians across the country. However, research shows that when role models in STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics) fields have seemingly unattainable careers, they actually make students less motivated to pursue STEM. The selection process was not nationally competitive and there’s no currently published plan or pathway for a young girl in Australia to follow in Bennell-Pegg’s footsteps. What message does that send to young people? It might discourage them from pursuing careers in space. We shouldn’t ignore the fact many Australians would support sending an astronaut simply because it’s exciting. That is a legitimate foundation for policy – after all we fund the arts, entertainment industry and sport – but we should also recognise many Australians would not agree with such spending when it comes to space. Unanswered questions remain If we want to send an astronaut to space, the Australian public should know precisely what the tangible benefits are – to them, their economy and their sense of what Australia stands for. A key final question is: what next? There are currently no plans for Australia to send a second astronaut to space after Bennell-Pegg. Not only does this limit the pathway for future Australians to go to space, but also undermines the arguments put forward for an Australian astronaut. If the benefits are so tangible and important, we wouldn’t only do it once. articles.author: Nick Ames at the Etihad Stadium
articles.content: For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne. Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ed Aarons at Emirates Stadium
articles.content: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jen Sherman
articles.content: The US has more big chains but in Australia produce is better quality – and bread doesn’t taste like cake I poked. I pulled. I looked in confusion at the head of garlic I was holding, wondering why the cloves weren’t coming apart. When I dug my nails in and finally broke out a clove, its skin was pierced and there were scratch marks in the flesh. It had only been a few weeks since I moved back to Australia from the US, after a 10-year stint in San Diego; only a few weeks since I cooked with garlic cloves. Surely I hadn’t lost finger strength that quickly? Turns out, it wasn’t me. It was the garlic. Since that first Australian head of garlic, I’ve discovered that Australian garlic is tighter than the US variety. Over there, a few gentle rubs prise the cloves apart. Here, you’ve really got to put some effort in – I suspect that’s why you can buy a packet of garlic cloves in supermarkets and I never saw such a product in the States. Garlic in Australia is more expensive, too. Continue reading...

articles.content: The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting? That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous. Continue reading...

articles.author: Benjamin Lee
articles.content: A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100th anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Sometimes, the beautiful game can make Football Daily feel old. Even Monday’s ostensibly old-school fixture between Brentford and Everton felt like the future destroying the past. The analytics-coded hosts prevailed 4-0 and James Tarkowski was dismissed by the VAR overlords for a challenge that would have been considered “firm but fair” on the muddy pitches of our youth. “I don’t think you can tackle like that in this day and age,” a misty-eyed David Moyes sighed after the game, before heading to the team bus to rewatch the Battle of Santiago . If Sunday was Gary Neville’s Sistine Chapel [ Monday’s Football Daily ], then his commentary on the Fernando Torres goal for Chelsea against Barcelona must be his David ” – Ronnie McMahon. Regarding Declan Hackett’s assertion [ Monday’s letters ] that Donald Trump will be helping his mate Mauricio Pochettino by ringing the FA to overturn Lenny Yoro’s red card, perhaps Poch should be careful what he wishes for: Trump may equally decide to get Michael Carrick reinstated, as he also has a bit of previous for that sort of thing” – Dexter O Riordan. In all the time that I have been watching football, I don’t think I have ever seen a player dismiss himself and be away down the tunnel before given a red card. Thanks James Tarkowski ” – Nigel Sanders. Brighton had only failed to win twice in the league since 5 September. A 1-1 draw with Leeds and a 2-0 defeat at Liverpool - their only opponents with double letters in their name. That bizarre hoodoo struck again at Hull on Sunday. Good good news for Seagulls fans is the only double-lettered encounters they have before hosting Hull in February are trips to Forest and Spurs. Even better news is that since that 1-1 draw with Leeds on 5 September, they have a 100% win record against sides without double letters and have not conceded a goal” – Dan Ashley (and no others). Continue reading...

articles.content: Content creators have produced hundreds of millions of hours of video game since its launch Grand Theft Auto ( GTA) VI became the largest video game release of all time last week and while it is hard to say exactly how many people are playing the game (current estimates say at least 30 million), there are plenty of other jaw-dropping data points we do know. Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Streams Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alyssa Mercante
articles.content: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.author: Aaron Timms
articles.content: For big stars, endorsing companies like Kalshi and Polymarket is just another day in the beautiful business of being – and staying – rich When Giannis Antetokounmpo announced he was taking an investment stake in prediction market Kalshi in February, the claim he made to accompany the announcement – “We all on Kalshi now” – sounded as absurd as the howls of outrage from sports lovers seemed universal. Nine months later, Kalshi’s grip on American fans appears murderously tight: notional monthly trading volume on the platform, the majority of which is taken up by wagers on sports, increased to nearly $100bn in October from $40bn in August, as the company gears up for yet another funding round at a rumored valuation of $65bn ahead of a potential IPO. Rival prediction market Polymarket, which relaunched in the US late last year after regulators shut it down in 2022, has seen similar growth over recent months. However righteous the disgust from fans on social media at the deepening incursion of these odious platforms into professional sport may be, their popularity seems only to grow. More perplexing is the widening circle of athletes like Giannis who’ve thrown off whatever shame might once have come from association with these businesses and given them their full-throated support. The line between role model and shill in professional sports is now essentially non-existent. Pete Sampras, a man so private in retirement it can often seem like his entire tennis career was a collective hallucination, released an ad for Kalshi during this year’s US Open after two decades largely out of the public eye. José Mourinho trousered a brick of Kalshi cash this summer in exchange for a gambling promo during the World Cup. The prediction market machine now sponsors Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart’s Roommates Show, on which the recently crowned pair of NBA champions begin every episode dutifully informing us that their amazingly dreary podcast is “presented by Polymarket, the top prediction market”. LeBron James will make more from his recently announced partnership with Polymarket – $15m a year – than he will from playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. Somehow we’ve arrived at the point where it’s bigger news if a professional athlete takes a firm stand against the prediction markets, as Victor Wembanyama recently did , rather than pockets the cash to endorse them. Continue reading...

articles.content: Winger has not played for the USMNT since the World Cup and believes good club form is his route back into the squad This was the USMNT’s summer. By extension, it was also that of the 26 players selected by Mauricio Pochettino to represent the nation at a home World Cup. It didn’t live up to expectations for all of them, and certainly not for Timothy Weah. “Obviously this summer wasn’t the best for me,” he says. Weah was one of eight players in the squad to have started all four of the US’s matches in Qatar in 2022. He remained a regular heading into this tournament but would ultimately start only one game in a campaign that came to an end at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 . “In every career you have moments where you’re a bit down, and you’re a bit in your head about things. I think the World Cup was definitely that for me,” Weah says. “On a personal level, I had to take a back seat and figure out where my place was in the squad.” Continue reading...

articles.content: Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The government will save more than it spends, says Jim Chalmers , but it won’t be a “slash and burn” budget update. Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo). There’s still a fair bit of work to do to finalise it all, but we’ve made enough progress to be confident that at this stage there will be a modest net save in the budget. We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. But we haven’t focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update. They will be substantial, as I said. These are serious times. You can see in the quite extraordinary reaction on the stock market just how volatile global markets are right now. I think it’s a bit of a symbol of the quite extraordinary volatility, unpredictability that we’re seeing play out in markets in the AI sector, but more broadly as well. Continue reading...

articles.author: Beejay Silcox
articles.content: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...

articles.content: The Australian government has secured an agreement with the Greens to guarantee passage of its long-awaited digital duty of care bill . The bill puts the onus on big-tech companies to address foreseeable online harms. Announced on Tuesday, the deal includes a number of measures to strengthen the bill, including bigger fines for platforms (to as much as 5% of global revenue) and a private right for people to sue the companies that breach their duty of care. Federal Minister for Communications Anika Wells acknowledged that it’s impossible to “cure” the internet of its ills. But she emphasised the digital duty of care bill provides basic safety standards that have to date been lacking. She described the package as “ seismic reform ”. What exactly is a ‘digital duty of care’? At its core, the bill requires the person responsible for an online service to ensure – as much as is reasonably practicable – a safe online environment . That phrase is borrowed from workplace health and safety law, and the logic is similar: rather than waiting for harmful content to be reported and taken down, platforms must identify the risks their services create and act to reduce them. The duty replaces the existing industry codes – which Wells described as “ drafted by big tech for big tech ” – as well as the eSafety Commissioner’s Basic Online Safety Expectations . Under the new bill, platforms would have to complete annual written risk assessments, keep them for six years and produce them to the eSafety Commissioner on request. The legislation has been years in the making. A statutory review of the Online Safety Act, delivered in October 2024, made 67 recommendations to strengthen the law. Its central one was a single, overarching “duty of care”, which the government committed to. After nearly two years, the government released an exposure draft in September, the headline feature of which was an “ off switch ” for personalised, algorithm-driven feeds for users. The bill was introduced to parliament on October 15. A Senate committee then reviewed the bill, receiving 182 submissions. Last week, it released its recommendations, which included a civil right of action and an exemption for low-risk services, such as small business websites. It backed passage of the bill, subject to its recommendations. What are the new changes? Wells outlined seven new changes to the bill as part of the government’s deal with the Greens: a private right of action, allowing individuals and groups to sue platforms that breach the duty stronger privacy protections expanded powers for eSafety to remove nudify services the naming of addictive platform design features as a specific risk that platforms must assess a clarified definition of “hostile attitudes to women”, which Wells said targets content promoting hatred, violence and threats, not disagreement with feminism a rule-making power to create an external dispute resolution pathway higher fines for violations of the law. The penalty change is the headline amendment. The bill already carried a maximum penalty of about A$109 million for companies found to have breached the obligation. The amendment adds an alternative penalty of up to 5% of global revenue. Among jurisdictions with similar laws, this would place Australia between Canada at 3% and the European Union at 6%. The Greens had sought 10% . The dispute resolution pathway is what the Greens call a pathway to an independent ombudsman for big tech. It creates a three-tiered option for social media users to bring complaints of harms against tech companies. First, they can turn to the platforms’ internal complaint process. If that fails, they can complain to a yet-to-be established tech platform ombudsman. Then if that fails, they can use the private right of action to go to court. The duty of care law would go into force after a 12-month transition. The government has confirmed low-risk, small businesses will be exempted from the law through rules, rather than in the bill itself. A significant shift There are several reasons why the changes to the bill are significant. First, the private right of action changes who enforces the law. Until now, online safety regulation in Australia has depended almost entirely on the eSafety Commissioner’s resources and priorities. A statutory duty that individuals and groups of people can use to sue means platforms face litigation risk, as well as regulatory risk. That matters because suing platforms has been difficult. For example, Australian mining magnate Andrew Forrest’s case against Meta over scam advertisements had to be pursued in a US court. Wells argued that Australians have previously had to attach claims to existing laws in order to sue. The new law would create a cause of action that does not currently exist. However, she said she expects it to be used rarely. Much will depend on how the courts approach causation in these types of cases, and on whether those financially backing litigation see class actions against platforms as viable. Second, the revenue-based fine raises the stakes with Washington. Wells said she met the US ambassador on Tuesday morning and acknowledged “points of difference” on this clause. She noted that courts elsewhere have rarely imposed maximum penalties against companies. The 5% figure is a ceiling, not a starting point. Third, the politics have changed. The Coalition opposes the bill, and Wells noted it will be the first online safety law to pass without bipartisan support. Online safety has been a rare area of consensus in Australia in the past. If the Coalition votes against the law, it is more exposed to being unwound, or simply under-resourced, after a change of government. Much of the detail is still to come. The dispute resolution scheme, the small business exemption and the treatment of addictive design all depend on rules yet to be written and on eSafety’s judgement. Regardless, with the passage of the bill now secured, the duty of care will shift responsibility to the companies that build these services. Rob Nicholls is a member of the University of Sydney Centre for AI, Trust, and Governance. He receives funding from the ARC. He made a submission to, and appeared before, the Senate committe.

articles.author: Adrian Horton
articles.content: The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney and 1923’s Michelle Randolph try their best, but this chaotic cross-country journey is not worth taking Credit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?) Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain-free bikini waxes”. Due to said budget cuts, both have a week to land “a book so big it makes Harry Potter look like a Buzzfeed listicle” for only one to keep their job. What are two LA workaholics going to do on Christmas but take meetings in New York? Continue reading...

Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. articles.author: Nadia Khomami
articles.content: The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own. Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”. Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.author: Jonathan Wilson
articles.content: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...

articles.content: Just outside Bundaberg is Sunnyside, a former sugar plantation owned by the family of former federal Labor MP Brian Courtice for more than a century. Between the 1860s – the decade the emancipation proclamation was signed in the United States – and the 1910s, at least 62,000 Pacific Islanders were coerced, tricked or kidnapped to provide labour on Australian sugar cane plantations. The term 'blackbirding' to describe this practice was taken from the African slave trade. At least 15,000 Islanders died on the cane fields, succumbing to overwork, malnutrition or exposure to diseases brought to Australia from Europe Continue reading...

articles.content: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alexis Petridis
articles.content: The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along. The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that an increasingly rosy view of rock history was abroad: the 90s also saw the rise of the heritage rock magazine, the expensively packaged retrospective box set and, indeed, of Britpop, an entire genre more or less predicated on evoking vague memories of the past, as if something of its magic might rub off through imitation. Continue reading...

articles.content: After some satirical experiments with the ‘disgusting’ AI, the photographer has returned to his first love with a book of contact sheets from his celebrity shoots. ‘I wish we could go back and stop everything changing,’ he says “I hate AI,” says Rankin. “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.” His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.” Continue reading...

articles.content: Irina/Getty Images Have you ever wondered why restaurants include outrageously expensive bottles of wine on their menus? Often, those bottles aren’t expected to sell. Instead, they make the other wines seem better value even if they are still overpriced. By changing the context of the decision, the out-of-reach expensive option can nudge customers towards wanting the cheaper option more. Marketers use similar tricks all the time. A holiday package that’s sold out, a premium subscription nobody really wants, or a product that’s clearly overpriced can all influence how we perceive the alternatives around them. Behavioural economists call these influences “decoy effects” . They reveal that decisions are not always rational based on absolute value. Instead, they are often shaped by the options available at the time. Humans aren’t the only animals making decisions. Every day, wild animals weigh up risks and rewards: whether to investigate a novel object, where to forage, or whether entering a trap is worth the potential danger. That got us wondering: could a decoy influence a rat? That was the subject of our new study, published today in The Journal of Applied Ecology . The problem with trapping rats Rats are among the world’s most successful and adaptable animals. They damage crops and infrastructure, spread disease, threaten native wildlife and cost economies billions of dollars every year in damages and pest control. Despite more than a century of innovation and thousands of patented trap designs, trapping still depends on one crucial step: the animal must choose to enter the trap. This seemingly simple decision is often where pest control programs fail. Many rats are naturally cautious around unfamiliar objects, a behaviour known as neophobia . A trap may contain attractive food, but if the perceived risk outweighs the reward, a rat may simply refuse to enter. Researchers and pest managers have traditionally tried to solve this problem by improving lures, making traps more appealing, or reducing fear of the trap itself. We explored a different possibility. Instead of changing the trap, could we change the rat’s perception of its options? An irresistible snack just out of reach To test this idea, we worked with wild black rats ( Rattus rattus ) in bushland around Sydney. We set up tracking tunnels which work much the same way as traps but the animals are free to leave. Outside some of the tunnel entrances, we placed a highly desirable peanut butter bait ball inside a steel mesh container. Rats could see and smell the peanut butter, but they couldn’t eat it. In effect, we created a “phantom decoy” – a tempting option that was present but unattainable. The idea was borrowed directly from behavioural economics. If the highly desirable but inaccessible food changed how rats perceived the available food inside the tunnel, rats might be more willing to enter. A surprising result The results were striking. Rats were 83% more likely to enter tunnels containing a basic food reward when the inaccessible “phantom” food was present. To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that a “phantom decoy” effect, a phenomenon well documented in human decision-making , can be used to influence trap-entry behaviour in a wild mammal. The decoy itself could never be eaten. Yet its mere presence changed the rats’ decision-making behaviour. Importantly, our experimental controls showed that placing the same inaccessible food inside the tunnel didn’t increase entry rates, nor was the effect simply due to the extra food attracting more rats to the area. The increase in tunnel entry only happened when the inaccessible food was positioned outside the tunnel, suggesting it changed how rats evaluated the option of entering. This suggests rats weren’t simply responding to the amount of food available. Instead, their decisions were influenced by how the options were presented. While we can’t know exactly how a rat experiences these choices, the findings show that altering perceived alternatives can substantially influence how rats behave. What this could mean for pest control The practical implications are potentially significant. Pest managers often encounter animals that investigate traps or bait stations but refuse to enter. This problem occurs at every scale , from failed island eradications to backyard rats that seem impossible to catch. When lures alone aren’t enough to overcome an animal’s reluctance to enter, changing how it perceives its options may be an effective alternative. Our study suggests a relatively simple and inexpensive way to encourage animals to enter traps: add a highly desirable but inaccessible food option outside the trap entrance. Importantly, this approach doesn’t require a new trap design, sophisticated technology or costly equipment. It simply changes the decision-making environment. Beyond rats The findings also raise a broader question. For decades, behavioural economists and psychologists have documented decision-making biases in humans. Increasingly, evidence suggests that some of these principles may extend beyond our own species. Animals, like humans, constantly make choices under uncertainty. Understanding those choices could unlock new ways to manage pest species , conserve threatened wildlife and improve animal monitoring. Sometimes, the best way to get an animal to choose option A may not be to make option A better. It may be to add option B.
